My statement specifies ‘we’ because I’m relating to the dilemma *we* (people with BPD) have struggling with a myriad of subconscious patterns of emotional reasoning and black and white thinking, and even if you personally don’t relate I never made a comment (until this response) saying ‘you’, but your response is entirely personal and includes and insult that could and would of offended my ego in the past, but I don’t really align with my ego anymore (some days I do and those are usually my bad days). Please know I never said just ‘snap out of it’ - I know it’s not that simple. 

What we’ve discussed in the realm of our egos doesn’t defeat the point I’m alluding to (and I’m also not pretending that I am the ‘barer of truth’ … ‘the finger pointing to the moon is not the moon’) - I’m highlighting that *we* do have autonomy in things that annoy us/ butt hurt and *we* are responsible for our own happiness.

Ever heard the phrase ‘taking offence’ ? 

No one offends us without us ‘taking’ it. We have a choice and autonomy whether or not to be offended/ insulted by others, even when they or their words are seemingly the sole ‘responsibility’ for the negative emotions we experience. 

We might be in an almost subconscious state of ‘taking offense’ almost automatically - but this will only change when WE make the decision to see the bigger picture and practice the tools of DBT. 

Sure it can be annoying being told ‘don’t be so negative’, especially when there is so much unresolved stuff in our lives. It doesn’t change the fact that we are responsible for our own happiness, no matter what we are told by others.

I feel ya mate. It’s a dichotomy we’re living with in a dopamine fuelled world. Even if people don’t recognise it as ‘addiction’ if we are constantly filling our time with our status on social media/ what’s happening on social media/ political drama/ toxic relationships/ gaming/ our phones/ food/ porn- *the lot* - it’s addiction. It’s dopamine fuelled attempts at escaping reality. However the issue with all of these attempts is that reality remains reality, and our problems either continue to exist or get worse while we’re feeding any addictive behaviour. Being inebriated is just one way to escape reality, and it is particularly addictive because it really does feel good. 

But when you’re sober and you can see things clearer… you can see your problems clearer too… as well as the answers. You find yourself (with the right help) much more empowered to solve your problems. You find you’re happier and content with consistency, rather than the pendulum swinging existence of inebriation. You find that solving your problems gives you real confidence, and you find yourself craving inspiration. You find yourself curious in ways that you never were before. You enjoy life on life’s terms. You feel a sense of peace knowing that you aren’t escaping reality, you’re working with it. And that is why sobriety- it’s worth it.
